name: Updating Two-Dimensional List (Case 3)
description: Construct a program that initializes a 2x4 two-dimensional matrix that has multiples of 10 from 10 to 80 for entries, updates the last row to a list holding values 1,3,5,7, then sets the second element of the first row to be 8, and finally prints the matrix.
code:
#Step 1: Define a 2x4 two-dimensional list 
matrix = [[ 10, 20, 30, 40 ],
          [ 50, 60, 70, 80 ]]
#Step 2: Update the two-dimensional list 
matrix[1] = [1, 3, 5, 7]
matrix[0][1] = 8
#Step 3: Print the list
print(matrix)

commentList: Purpose: This line starts creating the 2x4 two-dimensional list named matrix so you have the initial grid of values the rest of the program will update and print.

Syntax breakdown: The outer square brackets [...] define a list whose elements are themselves lists. Each inner list (e.g. [10, 20, 30, 40]) is a row. Commas separate elements inside a row and also separate the two rows from each other.
Line continuation: The assignment spans two physical lines in the source (line 2 and line 3) but is valid because the inner brackets allow implicit line continuation, so you don't need a backslash.

Common errors and misconceptions: Make sure you close all brackets and put a comma between the two inner lists. Using parentheses () would create tuples (immutable), and braces {} would start a set or dictionary (not a 2D list), which would break later indexed access.

Indexing/mutability note: Because you used nested lists, you can later change whole rows or single elements (for example matrix[1] = [...] or matrix[0][1] = 8). If rows have different lengths, you risk IndexError when accessing expected columns.

Best practices: Use a clear variable name like matrix, keep consistent spacing for readability, and prefer list literals for small fixed data. For larger or generated grids, consider building the rows with a loop or comprehension to avoid manual errors.

commentList: Purpose: This line replaces the entire second row of the matrix with the list [1, 3, 5, 7], so after this assignment you will still have two rows but the row at index 1 will contain those new values.

Syntax and meaning: matrix[1] accesses the element at index 1 (the second row) of the outer list; the = operator assigns a new value to that element; [1, 3, 5, 7] is a list literal. Together they make matrix[1] reference the new list.

Potential errors and misconceptions: Don't expect this to change a single cell—this replaces the whole row. If your matrix had fewer than two rows, matrix[1] would raise an IndexError. Also be aware that assigning a list stores a reference to that list; if you reuse the same list object elsewhere and then mutate it, those changes will show up in all places that reference it.

Best practices: Make sure the new row has the intended number of columns (here 4) so your matrix shape stays consistent. If you only want to change one element, use matrix[1][col_index] = value. If you need an independent copy of an existing list, create a copy (for example with list(original) or original[:]) before assigning.

commentList: This line sets the second element of the first row to 8, so you directly make matrix[0] (the first row) change from [10, 20, 30, 40] to [10, 8, 30, 40], fulfilling the program requirement to set that element to 8.

Breakdown: matrix[0] selects the first row because Python lists use zero-based indexing, the following [1] selects the second column inside that row, and the = 8 assigns the new value 8 into that position.

Common mistakes to avoid: if you used matrix[1][1] you would change the second row instead; using parentheses like matrix(0)[1] is invalid syntax; if the chosen indices are out of range you will get an IndexError; and if matrix[0] were a tuple you would get a TypeError because tuples are immutable.
Behavior note: this assignment mutates the existing list in place, so any other references to matrix or its first row will see the updated value.

Best practices: you should ensure the matrix has the expected dimensions before assigning (e.g., check lengths or use constants for row/column indices), add a short comment if the index meaning is not obvious, and avoid magic numbers by naming index constants when the code grows more complex.

commentList: Purpose: You call print(matrix) to display the final, updated two-dimensional list so you can verify the changes made in previous lines.

Syntax & semantics: You are using Python's built-in print function with the variable matrix as its single argument; print converts the nested list into a textual representation and writes it to standard output.
What you'll see: You should see the nested-list representation showing both rows, for example [[10, 8, 30, 40], [1, 3, 5, 7]], which reflects the updates you made.

Common errors & misconceptions: If matrix is not defined you'll get a NameError; forgetting parentheses (print matrix) is a SyntaxError in Python 3; printing does not change the data—print only displays it.

Best practices: If you want a clearer, row-by-row view, you can print each row in a loop (for row in matrix: print(row)) or use pprint for nicer formatting; avoid relying on print for program logic since it returns None.

If you execute this line, you will replace the first row of the matrix with the list [1, 3, 5, 7]. That means the subsequent step that changes a value in the first row will operate on this new list, not on the original multiples-of-10 row. The program will still run and print a 2x4 matrix, but the wrong row will have been updated. This line is plausible because it looks like a proper way to replace a row, but it targets the first row instead of the intended one. The key mistake is the incorrect index: you are updating a different row than required.
